venue.name: Kinsol Trestle
venue.description: The Kinsol Trestle is a restored timber railway trestle on the Cowichan Valley Trail near Shawnigan Lake, looked after by the Cowichan Valley Regional District. It is 187 metres long and stands 44 metres above the salmon bearing Koksilah River, has an unusual seven degree curve, and was finished in 1920 for the logging railway before being rehabilitated and reopened in 2012. It is open to walkers, cyclists and horse riders, and from the south parking lot it is about 1.2 km along a flat gravel rail trail. On site there are viewing platforms, benches, a picnic area, a kiosk and pavilion, a parking lot and year round toilets.

facility_notes.washrooms: There are accessible toilet facilities at the parking lot and on the north side of the Kinsol Trestle that are open year round.
facility_notes.lunch_space: The list of things on site includes a picnic area, benches, and a kiosk and pavilion. All of it is outdoors.
facility_notes.stroller_accessible: The trail is wheelchair accessible and is flat, wide, and surfaced with crushed gravel fines.
facility_notes.wheelchair_accessible: The trail is wheelchair accessible and is flat, wide, and surfaced with crushed gravel fines.

restrictions: Alcohol is not permitted in CVRD parks or trails, as per Parks Bylaw No. 738.
The natural environment of parks must be respected. No natural features are to be collected or damaged. All rocks, sticks, leaves, shells, etc. should be left in place as habitat.
No waste shall be left behind. All garbage, recycling and compost must be placed in the appropriate bin or taken with the group when leaving the park.

programs.name: Walk out to the trestle
programs.description: A self guided walk on the Cowichan Valley Trail out to the trestle and back. From the public parking area on Glen Eagles Road it is about 1.2 km each way on the old railway grade, which is flat, wide and surfaced with crushed gravel fines. The trestle can also be reached from the north along the same trail. There are viewing platforms, benches and a picnic area, and year round toilets at the parking lot and on the north side of the trestle. Nobody guides the visit and there is nothing published about interpretive talks or a staffed presence on site.
programs.what_children_do: Walk about 1.2 km on a flat gravel trail from the car park, then step out onto the plank deck of the trestle high above the river and look down into the ravine from the viewing platforms.
programs.our_note: Their own fact sheet puts the walk in from the car park at about fifteen minutes, so budget for the return leg on tired legs as well. The deck is high, open and exposed, and there is no shelter anywhere along the route if the weather turns.
programs.practical_summary: Toilets at the parking lot and on the far side of the trestle are open all year, and the route is flat gravel that takes wheelchairs and strollers. There is no indoor shelter and nothing is published about parking a bus, so it is worth a call.
programs.evidence: The Historic Kinsol Trestle is open to the public for cyclists, hikers and equestrians

programs.name: School field trip request
programs.description: The regional district treats any school visit to one of its parks or trails as a field trip that has to be requested in advance, and that includes the Kinsol Trestle. The request goes in online or on a PDF form, and it asks for the date and time, the number of students and supervisors, how many adults hold first aid certificates and how many vehicles are coming. Requests must arrive at least 30 days before the visit and late ones are not accepted. A request can be turned down if another booking already has the park, if the group would push the park past what it can hold, or if there was not enough notice. Schools also have to show proof of general liability insurance naming the regional district, with a minimum limit of two million dollars, unless the trip is already covered by the Schools Protection Program.
programs.what_children_do: The visit itself is the same walk out to the trestle. The form is the paperwork the adults do first.
programs.our_note: Get the form in more than thirty days ahead, because a late request is refused rather than squeezed in. Check with your school office that the district insurance covers the trip, since the region asks for proof before it approves.
programs.practical_summary: Same site facilities as any other visit, with year round toilets and a flat gravel trail. No cost, group size limit or bus parking is published for a school visit, so ask when you send the form.
programs.cancellation_note: The regional district says it can cancel an event or activity because of unforeseen circumstances and will not cover any costs to the school if it does.
programs.evidence: School groups must submit their application no less than 30 days before the proposed field trip.

images.alt: A long curving timber railway trestle seen along its deck, crossing high above a forested ravine with a narrow gravel path on the valley floor below.
Two people walk away along the plank deck of the trestle between wooden railings, with the timber structure curving off to the right and conifer forest on both sides.

gaps: Nothing about ages is published. There is no youngest age, no grade range and no advice on whether the height of the deck suits small children, so that has to be your own judgement.

No price is published for a school or group visit, and the site never actually says the trestle is free to visit. The only fees mentioned anywhere in the parks pages are for reserving picnic shelters at three other parks, which does not include this one.

No maximum group size is given. The request form warns only that the size of the group must match the capacity of the park, counting toilets, parking and how sensitive the ground is, so ask what number they will accept.

Bus parking is not mentioned. The site describes a public parking area about 550 metres down Glen Eagles Road from Renfrew Road, but says nothing about coach or bus access or how many spaces there are.
There is no rain shelter published beyond a kiosk and pavilion, and no indication of whether either is roofed or big enough for a class.

No guided walk, interpretive talk, ranger programme or school workshop is offered at the trestle. The regional district's school pages cover permissions and paperwork only, so anything educational has to be brought by the teacher.
How long a visit takes is not published. The site gives the distance as about 1.2 km each way from the south parking lot and their fact sheet calls it about a fifteen minute walk.
No coordinates are published on the page. Their map is a drawn image rather than an embedded map, so only the park address was recorded and the pin is left for geocoding later.
Neither photograph carries alt text on the site, so both descriptions were written after opening the images in a browser and looking at them.
The field trip request form and the teachers' guide are both labelled 2025, so check the notice period and the insurance limit still stand when you apply.
